items.title: Cơ hội để Việt Nam vươn lên trong chuỗi giá trị bán dẫn toàn cầu
items.summary: Triển vọng ngành bán dẫn tiếp tục được thúc đẩy bởi làn sóng AI và chuyển đổi số toàn cầu. Theo FedEx và Frost & Sullivan, thế giới dự kiến xy dựng hơn 2.000 trung tm dữ liệu mới trong giai đoạn 2026-2035. Sự phát triển của điện toán hiệu năng cao, mạng 5G và xe điện đang mở rộng nhu cầu đối với chip xử lý, chip nhớ cùng các giải pháp bán dẫn chuyên dụng. [...] Cùng với đó, hạ tầng nghiên cứu, nguồn điện ổn định và hệ thống logistics cần được phát triển đồng bộ. Đặc thù sản phẩm bán dẫn đòi hỏi độ chính xác cao, quy trình kiểm soát chất lượng nghiêm ngặt và thời gian giao hàng đáng tin cậy. Việc hoàn thiện các điều kiện nền tảng sẽ góp phần nng sức hấp dẫn đầu tư, đồng thời hỗ trợ doanh nghiệp trong nước tham gia su hơn vào chuỗi cung ứng. [...] Thành quả này cho thấy Việt Nam đã có những bước tiến cụ thể trong chuyển hóa năng lực nghiên cứu thành sản phẩm vi mạch. Dù chưa đồng nghĩa với việc làm chủ toàn bộ quy trình chế tạo bán dẫn, khả năng tự thiết kế chip chuyên dụng có ý nghĩa quan trọng, mở ra triển vọng phát triển các sản phẩm phục vụ an ninh, quốc phòng, công nghiệp và những lĩnh vực có nhu cầu bảo mật cao.

items.title: Doanh thu bán dẫn toàn cầu đạt kỷ lục 517,7 tỷ USD trong quý 3 - VnEconomy
items.summary:
Theo báo cáo mới đy của Hiệp hội Công nghiệp Bán dẫn Mỹ (SIA), doanh thu bán dẫn toàn cầu trong quý 3 ước đạt 517,7 tỷ USD, tăng gấp 2,5 lần so với cùng kỳ năm ngoái và tăng 24,1% so với quý trước.

Đy là lần đầu tiên doanh thu bán dẫn toàn cầu trong một quý vượt mốc 500 tỷ USD. Đáng chú ý, thị trường này đã ghi nhận mức tăng trưởng doanh thu khoảng 20% trong từng quý kể từ đầu năm. [...] Đà tăng trưởng này chủ yếu đến từ nhu cầu mua sắm đồng loạt các bộ tăng tốc AI và chip nhớ băng thông cao (HBM) của những doanh nghiệp vận hành các trung tm dữ liệu quy mô lớn.

Tính chung 9 tháng đầu năm, từ tháng 1 đến tháng 9, doanh thu bán dẫn toàn cầu đã vượt 1.219,5 tỷ USD, cao hơn 54% so với mức doanh thu kỷ lục 791,7 tỷ USD của cả năm ngoái.

Với tốc độ tăng trưởng hiện tại, doanh thu toàn ngành được dự báo sẽ vượt 1.600 tỷ USD vào cuối năm nay. [...] Trong các phn khúc bán dẫn, chip nhớ đang ghi nhận tốc độ tăng trưởng doanh thu nổi bật nhất.

Theo số liệu do Hiệp hội Công nghiệp Bán dẫn chu u phn tích, doanh thu chip nhớ toàn cầu trong quý 3 tăng 405,7% so với cùng kỳ năm ngoái. Trong khi đó, doanh thu chip logic, dòng chip đảm nhiệm các chức năng tính toán và điều khiển, chỉ tăng 61,9%.

Đà tăng trưởng vượt trội của chip nhớ chủ yếu xuất phát từ nhu cầu DRAM gia tăng, trong khi giá bán các sản phẩm cũng liên tục leo thang.

items.title: Anthropic and OpenAI are coming for the development workflow | InfoWorld
items.summary: This is clearly where the frontier labs are moving, even though they’ve all benefited from an industry that provided neutral spaces to build. For example, OpenAI developed Pando, a Git back end for its own monorepo, to handle more engineers and agents reading and writing code concurrently. Its engineers kept using Git. OpenAI retained compatibility with the protocol and client and contributed improvements upstream. That compatibility let it rebuild the back end around the way its engineers [...] This pressure to maximize profitability helps explain why frontier labs like Anthropic and OpenAI are aggressively adding functionality to own more of the developer’s workflow. On November 4, OpenAI announced an agreement to buy Pierre, the company behind Code Storage and the open source libraries Codex already uses to browse files and review changes. OpenAI wants Codex to be where developers work, from the first branch an agent creates through deployment of the application. There’s money in [...] OpenAI or Anthropic could build the place developers prefer to work. The question is what happens when a team likes that place and wants a rival’s agent for a particular job. Maybe a startup has built a tool that can track down the intermittent test failure that’s had the team stumped for a week. Give it access to the code and test history the team has authorized, and it gets a chance to prove itself. Ask the team to move its work to a new platform first, and it probably never gets to try.

items.title: RAG vs. Vectorless RAG, clearly explained!
items.summary:
RAG vs. Vectorless RAG, clearly explained!

In a standard RAG setup, documents are split into chunks, embedded, and stored in a vector DB. The query gets embedded too, and the top-k closest chunks go to the LLM.

The problem is that similarity and relevance answer different questions.

For instance, five annual reports from one company can likely follow the same template every year, and only the numbers can change.

So a FY2022 question can lie just as close to an FY2025 chunk, and the LLM might answer from the wrong year.

Cross-references introduce another problem. If a chunk mentions "see Appendix G" but looks nothing like the table in Appendix G, that table will never make it to the top-k.

Vectorless RAG drops the embedding model and the vector DB, and replaces similarity search with LLM reasoning instead.

The preprocessing step parses each document's layout into a ToC tree index. Every node holds a section title, its page range, and a short summary, and the whole tree fits in the LLM's context.

At query time, the LLM gets the query along with the tree. It reads the section titles and summaries and picks the few sections most likely to hold the answer.

For example, for a question about debt, it might pick the "Financial Summary" section and also "Appendix G", because its summary says the debt details are there.

The system then pulls those full sections and checks whether the evidence is enough.

↳ If it is, the LLM answers from the full sections, with page citations.
↳ If not, it goes back to the tree and opens more nodes.

The LLM also sees the chat history. So if you ask about assets and then follow up with "what about liabilities?", it goes back to the same report.

The trade-off is that every query now runs LLM calls over the tree.

Top-k vector search will be cheaper in that same run (although not guaranteed to be as accurate), and the tree only helps when documents have real structure.

So the two suit different data:

↳ Use a tree for long, structured documents like filings, contracts, and manuals.
↳ Stick with a vector DB for lots of short, unrelated text.

The diagram below depicts both flows.

If you want to dive deeper, I have also written a full breakdown of MIT's Recursive Language Models.

It covers why LLMs get worse as context grows and how RLMs let the model split a long document and work through it piece by piece.

Read it below.

items.title: Your RAG pipeline can lose the answer before the LLM even sees it.
items.summary:
Your RAG pipeline can lose the answer before the LLM even sees it.

Anthropic reported 67% fewer retrieval failures using contextual retrieval + reranking.

Here’s the architecture behind that number:

01 / Give each chunk its identity back

“Revenue rose 8%.”

Which company? Which quarter?

Before indexing, prepend a short explanation that connects the chunk to its source document.

02 / Search two ways

Embeddings capture semantic similarity.
BM25 helps find exact terms and identifiers.
Use both. Combine the results. Remove duplicates.

03 / Rerank the evidence

Finding something similar isn’t the same as finding the best evidence.

In the experiment, 150 candidates were reranked down to 20.

The reported retrieval failure rates:

→ Baseline: 5.7%
→ Contextual embeddings + contextual BM25: 2.9%
→ Add reranking: 1.9%

That’s a 67% relative reduction in retrieval failures—not a 67-point jump in answer accuracy.
Before your next model upgrade, try this:
Same corpus.
Same labeled questions.
Three retrieval configurations.

Compare retrieval misses, answer support, latency, and cost.

items.title: RAG vs. retriever-free RAG, clearly explained!
items.summary:
RAG vs. retriever-free RAG, clearly explained!

(powered by decision models like Jev)

In a standard RAG setup, documents are split into chunks, converted into embeddings, and stored in a vector index.

When a query arrives, the system embeds it and pulls the top-k chunks with the closest vectors.

A reranker then reorders those candidates against the query, and the best few go to the LLM as context.

The problem is that the similarity search decides what the LLM can ever see.

If the right passage never made the top-k, nothing later in the pipeline can bring it back, not even a strong reranker.

Retriever-free RAG, from a new Cornell and ASAPP paper, keeps the documents and the LLM but replaces similarity search with navigation.

The documents are organized as a document tree, like a table of contents, and a decision model (Jev 1.13) walks down it.

A decision model doesn't generate text. It reads one shared context and returns a probability for every yes/no question about it, in one forward pass per stage.

Here's how a query moves through the tree:

↳ Top documents: the model reads the query beside every candidate document, asks "Is this relevant?" for each, and keeps the best few.
↳ Top passages: it opens only those documents and asks the same question for every passage inside them.
↳ Most relevant? (optional): a single multiple-choice question reorders the top 20 passages (top 5 on Natural Questions).

Dropped documents are never opened, so their passages are never scored.

On Natural Questions (2.68M Wikipedia paragraphs), its top pick contained the answer 65.4% of the time. Embedding search plus an 8B reranker got 48.0%, and GPT-5 reranking got 60.8%.

The gain comes from ranking, not coverage. Embedding search's top 100 holds the answer more often than the navigated shortlist (98.4% vs 94.0%), but navigation is better at putting it first.

Median retrieval takes under 2 seconds per query, but each method was timed in a different setup, so it isn't a controlled speed comparison.

The main limit is that it needs a sensible hierarchy, and a document pruned early is gone for good. It also skips embedding search only at query time, since the Wikipedia tree was built offline using embeddings.

The diagram below depicts the complete flow.

- RAG retrieves by similarity, then reranks.
- Retriever-free RAG navigates a document tree with a decision model.
- The LLM answers from the top passages.

If you're building a RAG system, this is worth benchmarking against your current setup.

Here's the paper: https://t.co/U7cCcIfZV1

If you're new to decision models, I've quoted my full breakdown of how Jev works below.
